title: Turkey Agrees to Gradual Handover of Bashiqa-Zilkan Base to Baghdad, Extending Iraqi State Authority in Sinjar
subhead: On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi struck a deal to transfer Turkey's military base in northern Iraq to Iraq and to reassert Baghdad's authority in Sinjar, while the OECD sharply raised Turkey's inflation forecasts and the regulator revealed the scale of last week's $18 billion fund liquidation.

sections.heading: Iraq: Bashiqa-Zilkan Base Handover to Baghdad
sections.body:
President Erdogan and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi agreed on a gradual transfer of Turkey's Bashiqa-Zilkan military base in northern Iraq to the Iraqi government, according to Reuters and a joint statement issued after their talks at the Turkish House on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. The two leaders also reached an understanding on establishing full Iraqi state authority in Sinjar and on removing 'banned foreign armed groups' from the region, with media reports citing a target of completing the process by June 2027.

The deal pairs a Turkish military drawdown with a security commitment: the leadership pledged deeper security cooperation, and the agreement follows Iraq's broader push to rein in Iranian-backed militias and consolidate control over areas that host both Turkish forces and PKK-linked groups. Ankara has long operated inside northern Iraq against PKK targets in Qandil and Sinjar, where it has pressed Baghdad and Erbil to deny the group a foothold.
sections.whyItMatters: A Turkish agreement to vacate a major base on Iraqi soil is a real, if gradual, rebalancing of Ankara's northern Iraq footprint. It signals a security-for-sovereignty trade: Baghdad reclaims territory while Turkey extracts Iraqi commitments against PKK and 'outlawed' elements, and it could reshape how Turkey sustains cross-border operations going forward.

sections.heading: Economy: OECD Sharpens Turkey Inflation Forecast, Trims Growth
sections.body: The OECD sharply raised its 2026 and 2027 inflation forecasts for Turkey while cutting its growth projections for both years, Reuters reported on Wednesday. The revision signals that disinflation in Turkey is running slower than policymakers hoped, with the central bank's tight-money campaign yet to fully anchor price expectations. The downgrade to growth underlines the cost of that tightening at a moment when Ankara is juggling rebalancing, investor confidence and a fresh wave of fund liquidations.
sections.whyItMatters: The OECD's forecast move matters because it quantifies the trade-off at the heart of Turkey's current policy mix: external institutions see persistent inflation eroding growth into 2027, which pressures the central bank to stay restrictive even as the government courts investment and tries to calm markets.

sections.heading: Markets & Regulation: Scope of the $18 Billion Fund Liquidation
sections.body: Turkey's capital markets regulator said on Wednesday that almost half a million investors hold stakes in more than 100 investment funds worth around $18 billion that authorities ordered liquidated last week during a market selloff, Reuters reported. The disclosure is the first clear quantification of the crackdown's scale, extending a wider regulatory offensive that Ankara has also directed at fund and asset managers. The episode has reignited questions about investor confidence and the transparency of Turkish capital markets.
sections.whyItMatters: Half a million retail investors are now directly exposed to a regulator-mandated unwinding of over $18 billion in funds — a financial stability and trust test. How the liquidation is executed and how quickly investors are made whole will shape sentiment in Turkish markets and the credibility of the regulator's wider cleanup campaign.

sections.heading: Financial Crime: FATF Credits Turkey, Demands More on Illicit Assets
sections.body: The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) said Turkey has strengthened its fight against money laundering and terrorist financing but must do more to trace cross-border criminal proceeds and recover illicit assets, Reuters reported from its latest assessment. The verdict arrives as Ankara pursues its fund and asset-manager crackdown, and it gives Turkey a clear compliance checklist ahead of any shift in its grey-list status — a factor markets have watched closely since Turkey was placed under enhanced monitoring.
sections.whyItMatters: FATF recognition of Turkey's improved anti-money-laundering framework matters for investor perception, but the demand for better asset recovery and tracing keeps Turkey on a leash. Failing the next steps risks prolonging enhanced monitoring, which affects foreign capital flows and Turkish banks' correspondent relationships.

sections.heading: Energy: US Diesel Export Threat Pushes Turkey Toward India
sections.body: With the Trump administration considering ending US diesel exports, Turkey is looking to India as an alternative fuel supplier after India and the US became its top two diesel sources amid a push to diversify away from Russian imports, according to an analysis flagged in search results. The diesel squeeze sits alongside Turkey's broader energy rebalancing and comes as Zelenskyy urged India, China and Turkey to halt energy trade with Russia. Turkey's exposure to any US export cut makes its import mix — and its dependence on a shrinking pool of non-Russian suppliers — a live strategic and price risk.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkish refineries and transport fuel buyers rely on diesel imports, so a US export cutoff would hit prices and supply just as Ankara tries to reduce Russian dependence. India emerging as the fallback shows Turkey's energy security is increasingly shaped by second-tier supplier relationships rather than a single anchor.

sections.heading: Climate: Turkey's COP31 Presidency Sets Out Implementation Agenda
sections.body: Speaking at the UN, Turkey's COP31 president laid out an agenda to turn existing climate commitments into projects and measurable results, Reuters reported, with targets including raising electricity's share of energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035 and halving projected increases in municipal waste. The framing positions Turkey as a delivery-oriented host rather than a headline-setter, consistent with Ankara's push to be seen as a constructive global convenor during its conference presidency.
sections.whyItMatters: Turkey's COP31 presidency gives it a global stage to shape climate finance and implementation narratives ahead of the summit. The electricity-share and waste targets signal Ankara's willingness to bind itself to concrete numbers, which carries both reputational upside and the risk of being held to them.

bottomLine: Today's developments point to a Turkey simultaneously consolidating its regional role and absorbing the costs of internal stabilization. The Bashiqa-Zilkan handover is the standout move: a tangible, if gradual, Turkish military withdrawal from Iraqi soil bought in exchange for Iraqi commitments against PKK-linked groups and for state authority in Sinjar. At home, the picture is harder — the OECD is penciling in higher inflation and weaker growth, the regulator revealed half a million investors are tied up in an $18 billion fund liquidation, and the FATF wants more on illicit assets. Add a pending US diesel export threat and an activist COP31 presidency, and Ankara is managing a busy external portfolio while its economic policy faces a credibility test through 2027.
sources: Reuters, Cyprus Inform (Kiprinform), MSN, S&P Global/MSN analysis, Anadolu Agency context
